text:
COURT FILE
No.:  Toronto, Old City Hall, Information No. 04-120127970,

DATE:  January 26, 2007

Citation:
R.
v. Boujikian
, 2007 ONCJ 33

ONTARIO
COURT  OF  JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

HER  MAJESTY  THE  QUEEN

—  AND  —

BENJAMIN BOUJIKIAN

Before Justice J.W. Bovard

Heard on April 11, 25; May 9,31; November 16, 2006

Reasons for Judgment released on January 26, 2007

Mr. B. Warcop  ...........................................................   for
the Crown

Ms. C. Currie  ..............................   for the accused
Benjamin Boujikian

Bovard J.:

1
.

Benjamin Boujikian is charged with mischief under $5000.00 and with
theft under $5000.00 on December 12, 2004 in Toronto.

The
Issue

2
.

The issue is the credibility of the Crown witnesses and of the defence
witnesses.

Procedural
Background

3
.

The defence brought a
Charter
motion that was denied, and Mr.
Warcop, the Crown, told the court that he and Ms. Currie, defence counsel,
agreed that the evidence given by Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont during the motion
apply to the trial proper.

4
.

However, he did not mention the evidence given by Mr. Boujikian, or
officer Janes.  At page 4 of the November 16, 2006 transcript, pages 4 and 5,
the following exchange took place:

MR.
WARCOP:
Yes, Your Honour, I have spoken to my friend.  We've
agreed to allow the evidence from the
Charter
as it relates to Mr.
Snowdy, Mr. Clermont's testimony, to apply to the trial proper.  I understand
my friend wishes to further examine them.  At this point I would see no need in
calling them for the Crown, but they are both here available so my friend can
cross-examine them both.

THE
COURT:
Okay, so I'll order then on consent that all the
evidence on the voir dire, on the
Charter
, apply to the trial.

MS.
CURRIE:
Yes.

THE
COURT:
Okay, thank you.

5
.

It is clear that I assumed that the agreement was to include
all

of the witnesses’ evidence and that Ms. Currie agreed. Mr. Warcop did not
object to Ms. Currie’s agreement, therefore, I will proceed on the basis that
the agreement included
all
of the evidence given on the
Charter
motion,
and I will refer to it as it applies to the issue of proof beyond a reasonable
doubt.

Disposition

6
.

For the reasons stated below, I am persuaded beyond a reasonable
doubt that Mr. Boujikian is guilty of both mischief under $5000.00 and theft
under $5000.00 and he is found guilty.

Background

7
.

Track Parking Management (TPM) owns a parking lot on Wellington Street
West in Toronto, which is across the street from a parking lot where, the
accused, Mr. Boujikian works as a parking lot attendant. Just before the
incident, TPM switched to an automated fee collection system by installing
ticket machines in its parking lot. Shortly afterwards, it noticed a
substantial dip in revenues.  They hired a private investigator, Mr. Snowdy, to
investigate the problem. A colleague, Mr. Clermont, assisted him.

8
.

They set up video surveillance of the parking lot and saw Mr. Boujikian
remove a sign advertising fees for parking from in front of TPM’s lot. They
also saw him directing motorists into TPM’s lot and taking money from them to
park in the lot.

9
.

Mr. Snowdy arrested Mr. Boujikian for “public mischief” and handcuffed
him.  He put him in his car and called the police within several minutes. Mr.
Boujikian testified that he was held in handcuffs for two to three hours, but
Mr. Snowdy, Mr. Clermont and Officer Janes’ evidence indicate that it was about
one hour.

10
.

Mr. Boujikian said that he had an understanding with the attendant of
the TPM lot that when he left his lot, Mr. Boujikian could collect parking fees
from persons that parked there in his absence. He said that whenever the
attendant left the lot for a short time, he took off the parking rate signs to
let motorists know that he was not there, and that he, Mr. Boujikian, took off
the sign to conform with this practice.

The
Evidence

11
.

The Crown called Mr. Snowdy who said that he is a private investigator
and owner of Epic Protection Group Limited, a company that is licensed by the
Ministry of Public Safety and Security and Correctional Services.  During the
third week of November, 2006 TPM finished completely converting their parking
lot at 443 Wellington Street, from one that is run by an attendant to one that
is fully automated. After the third week of November, 2006 the full time lot
attendant was terminated.

12
.

On December 11, 2004 the management of TPM called him and told him that
their revenues had dropped by hundreds of dollars each night since December 1.
They said that one of their employees noticed that traffic cones had been
placed near their parking lot on December 10. TPM is the sole owner of 443 Wellington
Street, and no one else had authority to run a parking operation on that lot.
TPM hired him to investigate the reason for the diminishing revenue at the lot.
He was to investigate and take action. “Surveillance and apprehension” is what
he was hired to do.

13
.

On this evening he was working with Matthew Clermont, who is a municipal
law enforcement officer and works for one of Mr. Snowdy’s other companies. He
was there solely in the capacity of a by-law enforcement officer.
[1]

14
.

Mr. Snowdy went to the parking lot and set up video surveillance and a
few minutes before 10:34 p.m. he saw Mr. Boujikian go to the 443 Wellington
Street parking lot and remove the $5.00 rate card from an A- frame at the
entrance of the lot. He put it inside of the A-frame so that there was no
posted parking rate visible to the public. He removed the sign that faced the
traffic coming from the westbound lanes.

15
.

After Mr. Boujikian removed the sign he directed traffic into the lot.
This is an unattended parking lot and he saw Mr. Boujikian standing beside the
darkened kiosk, stopping cars entering the lot and conducting transactions with
the drivers.  This occurred eight to nine times.

16
.

He reviewed the video footage and testified that it recorded Mr.
Boujikian removing the parking rate card and putting it inside of the A-frame
and then stopping traffic as he described earlier.  It also recorded Mr.
Boujikian talking to the drivers that he was stopping and directing them into
the parking lot. He walked up to the darkened abandoned parking kiosk and
presented himself as the parking attendant.
[2]

17
.

The videotape did not capture Mr. Boujikian taking money from the eight
to nine persons that he directed into the lot, however, he saw him do this.  He
explained why he did not record him taking money from people at page 28 of the
transcript.
[3]

“…you can't have an infinite amount of cameras
processing. I picked the two most likely locations for two cameras. Mr.
Clermont's camera covered from the kiosk south to the - to the beginning of the
A-frame sign.  My camera covered the opening from the public access to the
street, and the A-frame sign up to the kiosk.  I had no indication that the
offender was going to stand south of the kiosk outside of the camera.”

18
.

Mr. Boujikian did not have the authority to be on TPM’s parking lot, so,
at 11:10 p.m. he crossed the street and confronted Mr. Boujikian, telling him
that he was a private investigator and that he was placing him under arrest for
public mischief and trespassing and handcuffed him.

19
.

He gave Mr. Boujikian his rights to counsel under s.10 (b) of the
Charter

twice from a laminate card that is standard issue to the police and is found in
their notebooks and then took him to his car. He called the police at 11:15
p.m. He said that Mr. Boujikian specifically said that he did not want to call
a lawyer or any other person. Rather, Mr. Boujikian wanted to settle the matter
with him. Mr. Snowdy cautioned him. The police came within an hour and dealt
with him for about an hour afterwards.

20
.

He handcuffed Mr. Boujikian because he felt that it was a confrontational
situation and that it was best for his own security.  That way Mr. Boujikian
wouldn’t be in control of the situation.

21
.

He said that Mr. Boujikian tried to buy him off with a large amount of
money that he had in his fanny pack.  He looked in the fanny pack, but he did
not search it. However, he saw that Mr. Boujikian had counterfeit or
photocopied parking receipts for the TPM parking lot.

22
.

Mr. Boujikian told him that he would pay back all of the money and asked
him how much he wanted.  Mr. Snowdy said that Mr. Boujikian made this overture
just before he gave him the secondary caution.  Mr. Boujikian offered him all
of the money that he had in his fanny pack if he would let him go. Mr. Snowdy
said that it looked like a lot of money.

23
.

Matthew Claremont testified that he works for Epic Parking Control,
which is a division of Epic Protection Group Services.  He was trained by the
municipality of Toronto as a municipal law enforcement officer, and is
certified as such by the City of Toronto.

24
.

He shares ownership of the security guard company and of a parking lot
company with Mr. Snowdy. His job is to check the parked cars in TPM’s lot to
see if they have a valid pay and display parking ticket.  On the night in
question he issued four or five infraction notices because the persons did not
have the proper parking permit displayed on their dashboards.  Several had the
same permit, but it was not the correct one. They appeared to be copies of old TMP
parking receipts from when there used to be an attendant running the lot.

25
.

He was working with Mr. Snowdy on the night in question and at 7:00 p.m.
he inspected the 443 Wellington Street West parking lot and established video
surveillance for it. He said there are three automated parking machines in that
lot.  At 8:30 p.m. he saw a male go to parking lots or parking areas on both
sides of 443 Wellington Street and put parking cones across the entrances.  He
saw this male interact with the traffic and direct them into the parking lot at
443 Wellington Street West.

26
.

He saw Mr. Boujikian move and close the A-frame parking sign in front of
the 443 Wellington Street West lot and then go out of sight.  The sign had the
parking rate for that lot. He said that the A-frame that Mr. Boujikian closed
up said: “Trak Parking Management Flat Rate $5.00”. Since it is automated, in
order to park there one has to pay with coins or a credit card at the machine
that they installed in their lot.  He said that the automated machines say in
small print what the parking rates are.

27
.

He saw Mr. Boujikian cross over to the 443 Wellington Street West
parking lot and stop a vehicle at the entrance.  He appeared to be collecting a
fee for parking and giving the drivers some type of paperwork.  Then the
drivers went into the parking lot.  He said that he saw money exchange hands
and a piece of paper be given to the drivers by Mr. Boujikian before they went
into the lot.

28
.

When he first saw Mr. Boujikian he was at the lot across the street from
443 Wellington Street West and it was obvious that he worked there as a parking
attendant.  Then he saw him come over across the street to the lot at 443
Wellington Street West parking.

29
.

Mr. Boujikian directed cars into the 443 Wellington Street West lot and
talked to the drivers.  However, this was not taped because the videotape
machine was set up in such a way that it did not catch this activity.

30
.

Shortly after 11:00 p.m., Mr. Snowdy arrested Mr. Boujikian and gave him
his s. 10(b)
Charter
rights from a notebook.  Mr. Snowdy took Mr.
Boujikian to the back seat of his car and talked to him.  Mr. Boujikian said
that he was working for Valet Pro’s across the street and that his boss was
Paul Gibbons and that they rented the lot across the street.

31
.

Mr. Boujikian was given the opportunity to call anyone he wanted, but
Mr. Boujikian said that he wanted the situation to go away and was trying to
negotiate with Mr. Snowdy.  Mr. Boujikian said, “can’t we make something out”
while Mr. Snowdy was trying to give him his s. 10(b) rights.  When it became
apparent that Mr. Snowdy was not going to make a deal with him, Mr. Boujikian uttered a couple of disparaging comments along the lines of,
"Well you work for blah blah blah Jews who own this place". Mr.
Clermont specifically remembered that they were anti-semitic comments, and he
confirmed that the owners are Jewish.

32
.

Mr. Snowdy read the s. 10(b) rights from a notebook or from a card.  Mr.
Boujikian said that he wanted to call his boss.  He said that he was a full-time
employee of the City of Toronto and was just trying to make some extra money
parking cars.  Mr. Boujikian was arrested for selling without authorization the
right to park in the lot at 443 Wellington Street West.

33
.

He saw that Mr. Boujikian had a sum of money in his pouch.  He offered
Mr. Snowdy money to “make the whole thing go away” and asked him if there were
something that they could do to make it go away.  He told them to take the
handcuffs off and he would make it worth his while if they could just deal with
the situation right then, however, Mr. Snowdy refused. The police arrived at
12:15 a.m. and that ended his involvement.

34
.

Officer Janes testified that he received a call at 11:37 p.m. to go to
the scene, and arrived there within 15 minutes of receiving the call, that is,
around 11:52 p.m.  He spoke to Mr. Snowdy who briefed him regarding the
situation.  Mr. Boujikian was in Mr. Snowdy’s car, sitting in the back seat
with his feet hanging out of the car.

35
.

He took custody of Mr. Boujikian and gave him his rights to counsel
under the
Charter
.  He did not want to call anyone.  He confirmed with
Mr. Snowdy that he was not violent and within five to ten minutes of his
arrival, told him to take off the handcuffs.  He was not surprised to see Mr.
Boujikian in handcuffs because he usually handcuffs persons that he arrests.
After releasing him, he did a CPIC check and determined that he did not have a
criminal record.  He charged him with mischief under $5,000.00 and released him
on a Promise to Appear. He was charged later with theft under $5,000.00 at the
behest of his supervisor.

36
.

That was the case for the Crown.

37
.

The defence called a character witness, Pasquale Carito, who works with
Mr. Boujikian at the Toronto Survey Department.  He has known him about six
years and they are good friends. He has met his wife and sister also. His main
contact with him is at work.

38
.

He said that Mr. Boujikian’s general reputation among his co-workers is
outstanding and that he is considered very trustworthy and honest.

39
.

Ms. Currie called Mr. Boujikian’s sister, Silvia Boujikian, to testify
about his ethnic background because Mr. Clermont testified that, in referring
to the owners of TPM, Mr. Boujikian made anti-semitic remarks. I did not
consider that whether he did or not affected the issues that I have to resolve
in this trial, but Ms. Currie argued that it went to the credibility of Mr.
Clermont, because if she could show that it was highly unlikely that Mr.
Boujikian made anti-Semitic remarks it would damage Mr. Clermont’s credibility.

40
.

In order to accomplish this she elicited the following evidence from
Ms. Boujikian:

Q.
Now,
Silva, you're Benjamin's sister, is that right?

A.
Yes,
I'm his older sister.

Q.
Okay.  Now, Silva Boujikian, what's - what's your
ethnic          origin?

A.
In general it's Armenian.  It's predominantly
Armenian, but on my father's side of the family it's more mixed.  My mother's
more pure Armenian, and on his side there's Macedonian and there's also Jewish.

Q.
Okay, so you have relatives then who are Jewish, is
that                                       right?

A.
Yes.

41
.

In cross-examination, she said that her father’s grandmother is Jewish.

42
.

Mr. Boujikian testified that he has worked part-time for about one and a
half years for Valet Pro’s Incorporated at a parking lot at 462 Wellington
Street in Toronto. He only works Saturday nights. He is also responsible for
the lot next door at 443 Wellington Street. He and his boss have an agreement
with the owner of the 443 Wellington Street lot that they can park their cars
there too. The TPM lot is across the street. He wears a uniform to identify
himself and his job is to take money from customers for parking. There is a
sign in front of the parking lot advertising their rates.

43
.

On the day in question, he arrived at work at about 9:15 p.m..  He
noticed that the person that usually works in the lot across the street was not
there.  The last time he worked there was the Saturday before. He had seen him
there since June, but he did not know his name because he had difficulty
remembering it as it was a Nigerian name.

44
.

Around 9:30 p.m. twelve vehicles from the C Lounge came and parked in
his lot and they each paid him $5.00 to park.

45
.

At about 10:10 p.m. he went to the lot at 445 Wellington Street to put
traffic cones in front of the entrance so no one could enter it. He did this at
the request of the owner of the parking lot.

46
.

He noticed that there were people parking in the lot across the street
but there was no one working there.

47
.

He
denied ever directing traffic into the TPM lot. He said that the cars that went
into their lot did not use the regular entrance:

…somebody created a false entrance, and it was the
driveway of 439.  They have a double driveway.  The second part of the double
driveway comes right adjacent to - to TRACT (sic) Parking, and all the parking
pylons mysteriously, I don't know how they did it, whoever it was, all the
parking pylons were removed, and all the vehicles were coming in from this new
created entrance.
[4]
(Sic
added)

48
.

He decided to stop and challenge them because they were just parking and
walking away. He described it this way:

A.
There were - there were
three cars that came back to back as a   group.  The - the three cars, they
parked, they were walking away, and I said, "Hold it."  I said,
"The attendant is not here right now," and they said, "Where is
the attendant?" They said, "We see the booth closed," and I
said, "Yeah, I came here too."  I said,” It might be a possibility he
might have gone to the washroom or something. I don't know," I said.  All
right?  But they said, "We don't want to leave our car you know. We don't
want to get a ticket," they said, right, 'cause the parking lots are known
notoriously if they don't have, despite anything in the windshield, that they
would be written a $30 or $60 parking ticket.

Q.
Okay, so what did you do?

A.
So I said to them, "Well, look," I said, "I have some
TPM tickets here                 that I found. If you like I said you can pay
me $5..."

49
.

He said that he found the tickets the week before on “the Sunday night”
when he was doing his rounds.
[5]
The
security staff of the C Lounge asked him to check for persons leaving the
Lounge with alcoholic beverages so they will not be given a ticket for a
violation of the liquor laws. He was doing this the week before at about 2:45
a.m. when he found 20-30 tickets on the ground. They looked like photocopies of
TPM parking tickets.

50
.

He planned to hold on to them and give them to the TPM attendant the
next week, which was the weekend of the day in question, because the TPM
attendant had left at “two o’clock” that night.

51
.

At 3:10 a.m., the morning that he found the tickets, he told his
supervisor, Ehor Oleksij, who just showed up, that he found them. Mr. Oleksij
told him that it was up to him to decide what to do with them. So he decided to
keep them until the following week when he was going to give them and the money
that he collected to the TPM attendant. He collected $5.00 from each of three
cars, and then a fourth car pulled in and he told them to give him $5.00. He
testified that he told the person, “I’ll give you a ticket, and I’ll transfer
the money over to the attendant when I see him, or his supervisor.”
[6]

52
.

But then he testified that he was going to give the money to his boss,
Paul, “ 'cause knowing that there's nobody there, or if he does show up, which
I was expecting him to show up, because I thought he was late showing up
for...” and he did not finish the sentence.
[7]

53
.

He said that he used to collect money for parking for the TPM attendant
when he had to go to the washroom.  Although he did not work for TPM, he had
charged persons before for parking in the TPM lot. There was an arrangement
with the TPM supervisor and he could only do it if he were authorized.

54
.

Mr. Warcop, the Crown, asked him if on the night in question he was
authorized to accept money on their behalf.  He said that if he were able to
call his boss, Paul, and if an arrangement had been made to allow this, yes, he
would have authorization. Then Mr. Warcop asked him again and he said that he
could not call his boss because he was in handcuffs and Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont
would not let him call.  Therefore, he could not confirm if he had permission
to accept money on behalf of TPM or not.

55
.

Then he said that, notwithstanding this, if the attendant was not there
he, “…would have the permission because he would come over and tell me, ‘Handle
these people, tell them to wait, or do something,’ or give him your tickets. If
the attendant was there, if let’s say the TRACT (sic) Parking attendant, if he
was there, no I would not.”
[8]
Then
he said that if there is no one working at the lot, he would, “Pretty well”
have permission to charge people for parking there because that is what they
have been doing. (Sic added)

56
.

Regarding what he did with the rate card, he admitted taking off the
card and putting it in the middle of the A-frame sign.  I will quote Mr.
Boujikian’s explanation of why he did that from page 103, lines 5-31.
[9]

A.

Basically it was this, as the three cars had pulled in, right, and I gave them
tickets, I was walking along the sidewalk to cross back onto my lot.  As I was
crossing, I saw one side of the A-frame.  At the east side of the A-frame,
where that $5 slot is, right in front of it somebody put a Cache Christmas
flyer - a big cardboard one.  I would say it's about three inches wide by six
or seven inches long, and they had put it and covered the $5 sign.  So as a
courtesy to the gentleman that usually is there, the attendant, I just pulled
out that side, the - the cardboard, and I threw it to the ground, then I went
to the other side and I'm saying, "How could this be," right?  Like
who - who's playing around here?  You know the alleyway is open, and all of a
sudden I see this cardboard here.  It wasn't there a moment ago when I walked
by, right?  Somebody is playing games.  So I said, you know to be on the safe
side, right, I don't know if the guy went to the washroom, he hasn't showed up,
I don't know.  So I said I'll follow what he usually does, right?  So instead
of taking the two sides off, I only took that one side off to indicate to the
regular clientele that comes to the parking lot that the parking attendant's
not here.  There's something not kosher.  So that was what my thinking was at
that night.  Now retrospect, looking back, maybe I did a mistake, but that time
what I thought was right, that's what I did, but after that I never went back
to their lot, nothing, because I stood there watching what was going on. I saw
cars coming in and out.

57
.

But he told the Crown in cross-examination
[10]

that he removed the sign that indicated the price to park, which is
inconsistent with having removed it because the price to park was covered up by
the Cache Christmas flyer.

58
.

Concerning conversion of TPM’s lot to an automated pay-and-display
system, he said:

A.
I saw the
pay-and-display, but I didn't see any sign indicating the pay-
and-display were operating.  Like usually if they're operating and have
a                     booth there, wouldn't you think logically they would put
a sign up and say                  "No more attendant," you
know,"The pay-and-display machine are operat-                 ing?"
There was nothing like that, and that attendant to me the week
before,              and the week before that, the week before that, didn't say
anything to me                  about you know he's going to lose his job, he's
going to be out whatever, no.              I saw the - the Saturday - the
Sunday morning before when he left around                  two o'clock that he
was going to be back.  He - he just waived and left.
[11]

59
.

At about 11:10 p.m., Derek Snowdy came up to him and grabbed him while
he was picking up some coffee cups.  Mr. Snowdy said he wanted to talk to him
and he flashed a card in his face.  Mr. Snowdy grabbed him by the arm and
twisted it behind him.  He told him that he did not have the right to block his
entrance to the lot the night before, but Mr. Boujikian told him that he had
not been there the night before.  Mr. Snowdy handcuffed him behind his back and
took him across the street to the parking lot.  He did not know who Mr. Snowdy
was.

60
.

Mr. Snowdy put him in a van and asked him his name.  Mr. Boujikian said
he wanted to call his boss and that when Mr. Snowdy asked him if he needed a
lawyer he told him that he did. Mr. Boujikian told him his name and Mr. Snowdy
called CPIC to check to see if he had a criminal record.  Matthew Clermont, Mr.
Snowdy’s partner, was standing relatively far away from them shouting that he
did not have the right to block the lot the night before.  Mr. Boujikian told
him that he had not worked the night before.

61
.

Mr. Boujikian said that they did not believe that he worked at the
parking lot. They called the police and while they waited they called his
boss.  When he was in Mr. Snowdy’s car he was alone and afraid, and he saw two
video cameras there. While he was in Mr. Snowdy’s custody in his SUV he was not
allowed to call anyone, although he asked Mr. Snowdy two times to let him make
a call.  He denied making any anti-semitic remarks while in his custody.  He
also denied offering them money to resolve the matter.

62
.

When the police came, he talked to one of the officers who took him to
the hood of the SUV and pushed him over it and frisked him.  He pulled out his
cell phone and told him to talk or he would be in trouble and he asked him what
he was doing there. He did not believe him either.

63
.

He said that he was handcuffed between two and three hours and was released
at 2:00 a.m.  At 2:06 a.m. he called his boss.

64
.

The police charged him with mischief for touching a parking sign in the
lot across the street from his lot and he was released on a Promise to Appear.
A couple of days later one of the officers called him and asked him to go to 14
Division because she had to give him a piece of paper.  When he went there they
charged him with theft under $5000.00.

65
.

That was all of the evidence.

The
Position of the Defence

66
.

Ms. Currie submits that credibility is the issue and that I should
consider that Mr. Boujikian does not have a criminal record.

67
.

She argued that Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont were hired by a rival
parking lot and that they had an agenda.  She said that Mr. Snowdy varied his
story and that he testified with fervor. Furthermore, they dealt with Mr.
Boujikian in a brutal and horrible way.

68
.

Moreover, a “Flat Rate” sign is inconsistent with a parking lot that is
an automated pay-and-display lot, especially since Mr. Clermont was checking
for expired tickets.  The removal of the sign cannot be mischief if the lot is
a pay-and-display lot.

Analysis

The
Law

69
.

On questions of credibility
D.W. v. The Queen
1991 CanLII 93 (SCC)
,
63 C.C.C.
(3d) 397
(S.C.C
.)
,
@
paragraph 11, states
the guiding principles for triers of fact.

First, if you believe the evidence of the accused,
obviously you must acquit.

Second,
if you do not believe the testimony of the accused but you are left in
reasonable doubt by it, you must acquit.

Third, even if you are not left in doubt by the
evidence of the accused, you must ask yourself whether, on the basis of the
evidence which you do accept, you are convinced beyond a reasonable doubt by
that evidence of the guilt of the accused.

70
.

Regarding the onus of proof, it is clear that the Crown bears the
onus of proving BRD that Mr. Boujikian committed these offences.  Mr. Boujikian
does not have anything to prove.

71
.

After having considered all of the evidence, counsel’s submissions and
the relevant law, I find as a fact that:

(a)

The TPM parking lot converted to an automated system during the third
week of November 2005, therefore, on the night in question, it was operating on
an automated, pay-and-display basis.

(b)

On the night in question, Mr. Boujikian, without authority, removed the
“Flat Rate” card that faced the west bound traffic, which indicated that it
cost $5.00 to park in the TPM lot, and he put it in the middle of the A-frame
that was in front of the lot, thereby making it impossible for motorists
passing from the west to see the advertised rate to park there.

(c)

Mr. Boujikian, without authority, directed traffic into the TPM lot.

(d)

Mr. Boujikian did not have the authority to take money from persons that
were parking in the TPM parking lot on the night in question.

(e)

Mr. Boujikian took $5.00 from four persons as a parking fee to park in
the TPM parking lot with the intention of keeping it for himself and did keep
it for his personal use.

(f)

Mr. Boujikian tried to bribe Mr. Snowdy in order to get him to
let him go without charge.

72
.

In addition, after considering all of the evidence, the applicable law,
and the submissions of counsel, I find that I do not believe Mr. Boujikian’s
testimony for the following reasons.

(a) His explanation regarding what happened
when he collected money from the four persons who parked in the TPM lot sounded
contrived.

73
.

He said that they told him that they did not want to leave there cars
there without a parking permit, and that he told them that he did not know
where the attendant was, but that, “Well, look,…I have some TPM tickets here
that I found. If you like…you can pay me $5.00.”  And he said that he told the
last person that pulled in that he would give her a parking permit and
“transfer the money over to the attendant when I see him,
or his supervisor.
”
(Emphasis added)

74
.

It is not believable that he would explain himself in this way to
strangers who just want to park in the lot.  What do they care, and what
difference does it make to the transaction that they know that he found TPM tickets,
or that he would transfer the money they give him to the attendant or his
supervisor? They are not going to check up on him later. And how would they
even know what TPM was? I find that in testifying in this manner, Mr. Boujikian
is presenting a highly implausible story of what he told these persons, which
coincides with the story that he told the court in order to bolster his in
court testimony.

75
.

In addition, he was inconsistent regarding what he was going to do with
the money because he testified that he was going to give the money to his boss,
Paul.

(b)
When he was cross-examined concerning whether or not he   had authority to
accept money from persons parking at the         TPM lot, his explanations were
confusing, rambling, and              sometimes inconsistent.

76
.

He said the following in this regard: (1) He had charged persons before
for parking in TPM’s lot because there was an arrangement with the TPM
supervisor and he could only do it when authorized.  (2) On the night in
question, if he were able to call his boss and if an arrangement had been made
to allow him to collect money for parking in the TPM lot he would have authorization
to do it. He said that he could not call his boss because he was in handcuffs.
However, he took the money before he was handcuffed.  If it were true that all
he had to do was to call his boss to find out if he had the authorization to
accept money from persons parking in the TPM lot, I would have expected him to
do it before he took the money from them.  (3) The attendant could authorize
him to accept money from persons parking in the TPM lot if he had to absent
himself for a short time, for example, to go to the washroom. (4) If there were
no TPM attendant working the lot, he said that he would, “Pretty well” have
permission to charge persons to park there because that is what they have been
doing.  If this were true, why would he have to call his boss to confirm it?

(c)
Regarding the “Flat Rate” card that he
removed from the

A-frame, his testimony was equally confused
and incon-

sistent in parts.

77
.

In one part of his testimony he said that he removed it as a courtesy to
the TPM parking attendant, because someone had put a Cache Christmas flyer over
the $5 sign. He wanted to “follow what he [the TPM attendant] usually does” and
instead of taking [both signs off] he only took off the covered up sign off “to
indicate to the regular clientele…that the attendant was not there”.  But in
another part of his testimony he said that when the TPM attendant has to absent
himself from the lot, he takes
both
signs off because they are easily
stolen and he asks him to monitor his lot until he gets back.

78
.

It does not make sense that if he wanted to alert the regular clientele
that the TPM attendant was not there he would only take down one sign.  How
about the regular clientele coming from the other direction?  I find this explanation
makes no sense and it is unbelievable.

79
.

He also told the Crown in cross-examination that he removed the sign
that indicated the price to park, which is inconsistent with having removed it
because the "$5” was covered over by the Cache Christmas flyer.

80
.

Ms. Currie argued that:

So, number one, my
submission is that what Mr. Boujikian says, trying to cope with the fact that people
are coming and parking, and he thinks that this other attendant has gone
somewhere and is going to return, and that this attendant is supposed to be collecting
a $5 flat rate as it says on the sign, and that he's somehow gone to the
washroom, and that he's going to step into the breach so to speak and collect
some money, that that makes sense given his experience with the system down
there.
[12]

81
.

I do not believe that Mr. Boujikian thought that there was an attendant
at the TPM lot because he said that, normally, when the attendant leaves the
lot to go to the bathroom he takes off both rate signs. The fact that the signs
were on the A-frame would have indicated to him that, according to what he
testified normally occurs, there had been no attendant there to take off the
signs.

82
.

Moreover, he testified that he told one of the persons from whom he took
money to park in the TPM lot that he was going to give the money to the
attendant or his supervisor.  Why would he mention giving the money to the
supervisor if he thought the attendant was only gone temporarily?

83
.

I do not believe that he took the sign down because that is what the
attendant used to do when he went to the washroom to let prospective clients
know that he was not there. If, as Mr. Boujikian testified, on these occasions
the TPM attendant authorized him to collect money while he was in the washroom
from persons that wanted to park in the TPM lot, would he take down the rate
card sign that told the clients how much to pay?

It makes
no sense, and I find that he concocted this story to furnish himself with a
viable excuse for having taken down the sign. Ms. Currie herself did not
understand the logic of the attendant doing this.
[13]

(d)
The
fact that Mr. Boujikian tried to buy off Mr. Snowdy is cogent

evidence
that he is guilty of these offences.

84
.

Neither Mr. Snowdy nor Mr. Clermont was successfully impugned on this
point and I accept their evidence in this regard. They both made notes of the
event and I find their evidence credible.

(e)
Mr.
Boujikian’s account of the length of time that he was in

custody
was a gross exaggeration and this damaged his credi-

bility.

85
.

Mr. Boujikian agreed with Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont that Mr. Snowdy
approached him and arrested him at 11:10 p.m. Mr. Snowdy said that he called
the police at 11:15 p.m. Officer Janes said that he received a call to go to
the scene at about 11:37 p.m. and arrived within 15 minutes, which would have
been around 11:42 p.m. He did not give the time at which he released him, but
from his evidence it appears that he kept him there for routine questioning
before releasing him on a Promise to Appear. There is nothing in the
circumstances that would have taken two to three hours as Mr. Boujikian
testified.

86
.

Mr. Snowdy, Mr. Clermont and officer Janes all took notes of these times
and, therefore, I find their evidence is much more believable on this point
than Mr. Boujikian’s. I find that he grossly exaggerated how long he was in
custody in order to paint Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont in a bad light as if they
were treating him unduly harshly.

(f)
Mr.
Boujikian’s evidence about wanting to call someone after Mr.

Snowdy
arrested him is unbelievable.

87
.

Officer Janes said that Mr. Boujikian did not want to make any telephone
calls when he asked him. This tends to confirm Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont’s
evidence that when asked if he wanted to call a lawyer, he said that he did
not.

Mr.
Boujikian testified that he told Mr. Snowdy that he wanted to make a call, but
they would not let him.

88
.

I do not accept his evidence on this point because Mr. Snowdy and Mr.
Clermont made notes in this regard, and office Janes, who is independent from
any likelihood of bias against Mr. Boujikian made notes and testified that he
did not want to call anyone when he asked him. I find that it is Mr. Boujikian
again doing all he can to portray himself as an innocent person being treated
horribly and in a brutal manner, as Ms. Currie submitted, which I do not find
to be the case at all.

89
.

For these reasons, I find that Mr. Boujikian’s credibility was severely
undermined. I not only do not believe Mr. Boujikian’s evidence, but neither am
I left in reasonable doubt by his evidence. The reasons given above for not
believing his evidence are cogent enough, in my view, to cause me not to be
left in reasonable doubt by his evidence.

90
.

In making the above determinations I considered the character evidence
of Mr. Carito who said that Mr. Boujikian has an outstanding reputation, and a
reputation for honestly and trustworthiness. However, in light of the problems
with his evidence pointed out above, I do not find that this evidence repairs
Mr. Boujikian’s credibility.

91
.

Now, I must ask myself if, “…on the basis of the evidence which [I] do
accept, [I] am convinced beyond a reasonable doubt by that evidence of the
guilty of [Mr. Boujikian]”.

92
.

I will turn to the other evidence by firstly referring to Mr. Snowdy and
Mr. Clermont’s evidence.  Ms. Currie argued forcefully that they are not
credible because Mr. Snowdy varied his testimony, and testified with fervor.
She submitted that they were employed by a rival parking lot, had an agenda,
and treated Mr. Boujikian in a brutal and horrible way. In other words, they
were out to get him.

93
.

Ms. Currie did not give any examples where Mr. Snowdy varied his
testimony and I cannot find any variances of any significant importance in any
relevant areas.

94
.

I observed Mr. Snowdy closely while he testified and I grant that at
times he was argumentative and difficult in cross-examination, but in fairness,
Ms. Currie subjected him to an intense cross-examination and accused him of
treating Mr. Boujikian very badly, so it is natural that he would try to defend
himself. I do not find that his fervor in testifying was such that it would
indicate dishonesty or unreliability.

95
.

I considered the possible bias that might exist because TPM was his
client.  However, I find little evidence that a bias exists that warrants me to
disbelieve his evidence.  He is a professional and he was hired to investigate
the short fall of revenue at the TPM parking lot and to apprehend anyone that
he saw stealing from them.  This does not automatically make his evidence suspect.
And I see nothing in it that causes me to doubt his veracity or reliability.
On the contrary, he is a trained investigator and kept good and accurate notes
of what happened. He recorded Mr. Boujikian on videotape. I find that he was
careful to recount the relevant facts in an accurate manner.

96
.

As for having an agenda and treating Mr. Boujikian in a brutal and
horrible way, I do not see any evidence of this, nor do I believe that to be
the case.

97
.

Ms. Currie emphasized that he was hired by a rival parking lot, but TPM
did not hire Mr. Snowdy to investigate Mr. Boujikian, or Valet Pro’s Inc., the
owners of the lot where he worked. They hired him to investigate why their
revenues at thier lot had dropped since they automated it. There is no evidence
that they, or Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont thought that the culprit was Mr.
Boujikian or his employer.

98
.

Similarly, regarding, Mr. Clermont, I do not find that Ms. Currie’s attack
on his credibility can be sustained. He too is a trained investigator, who took
careful notes in a timely manner of what happened. I detected no bias,
dishonesty or unreliability in his testimony.

99
.

Mr. Snowdy and Mr. Clermont testified in a straightforward manner that
was plausible. Neither was inconsistent or contradictory within his own
evidence, nor in relation to the other’s evidence, or to any other evidence,
except Mr. Boujikian’s. Ms. Currie subjected them to intense cross-examinations
and they both withstood it well. Their evidence was not undermined.  I find
them both to be quite believable and I do believe them.

100
.

Ms. Currie argued that there was no evidence to show when TPM automated
their parking lot.  I disagree with this, because Mr. Snowdy testified that TPM
hired him to investigate the shortfall in revenue in this lot since the third
week of November 2005, when they automated the lot.  This is credible evidence
and I accept it, because it is reasonable and logical that TPM would explain
the details of why they were hiring Mr. Snowdy and they were his clients so he
would know this.

101
.

Ms. Currie also argued that it is inconsistent to have a “Flat Rate”
sign if the lot is automated.  She also contended that it is not mischief to
remove the sign if it is a pay-and-display lot.

102
.

I do not think that this is necessarily so. The lot could be automated
and

charge a flat rate, one simply would have to purchase the ticket from the
machine for the rate prescribed. I also agree with Mr. Warcop’s argument that
the sign could have been simply advertising. He pointed out that as motorists
drive by they would see the flat rate sign, which informed them how much it
cost to park there.

103
.

In these circumstances it is sufficient to constitute mischief to remove
a “Flat Rate” sign from in front of the TPM lot, notwithstanding that it is a
pay-and-display lot. The owners obviously put the sign there to attract
customers and removing it renders the sign useless and constitutes mischief
under
s. 430 (1)
(b), (c) of the
Criminal Code
.
[14]

104
.

In addition, none of the witnesses said that the attendant showed up
during this incident. I think that is reasonable to infer that had the lot been
an attendant run lot, the attendant would have returned during the time that
Mr. Snowdy, Mr. Clermont and officer Janes were interacting with Mr.
Boujikian.

Disposition

105
.

For the reasons stated above, I am persuaded beyond a reasonable doubt
that Mr. Boujikian is guilty of both mischief under $5000.00 and theft under
$5000.00 and he is found guilty.
